rv.q: Ian McKellen and Patrick Stewart find plenty of consoling comedy in two masterpieces of existential despair.
This was not the trickery of surface caricature but the mystery of deep acting at work.
Both actors, neither one immune to the lure of excess showmanship, are terrific -- stylish, disciplined, strikingly different
These shows are an irresistible celebration of two actors’ love affairs with their scripts.
If you have to pick one, “No Man’s Land” is the way to go.

McKellen and Stewart's joyous pairing is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to see and hear these two knights of the theater clown and caper and kvetch their way through what's been called the most significant play in the English language.
As played by Ian McKellen and Patrick Stewart, Beckett's iconic hobos suggest two old vaudevillians, well past their prime but not incapable of recapturing that old magic.
The stars behind Magneto and Charles Xavier go head-to-head again and light up Broadway in Harold Pinter’s “No Man’s Land” and Samuel Beckett’s “Waiting for Godot.”

It is, nevertheless, sheer folly to build a revival of Godot, one of the most challenging plays in twentieth-century drama, on a pair of actors with little theatrical experience and limited technical skills.
Director Sean Mathias has staged, almost choreographed, a dazzling cast in a haunting performance of a poignant, classic play.

cn.t: McKellen and Stewart bring star power and disciplined performances to Beckett's existential classic, mining humor and pathos under Sean Mathias's direction. Critics mostly charmed, though some question the stars' limited theatrical technique.

vs.sum: A beautifully restored theater with a stunning Tiffany-inspired interior. The 2021 renovation transformed restroom facilities from among Broadway's worst to a model for the industry, with modern bathrooms on every public level.

acc.note: Elevator to Mezzanine, Balcony, and lower level restrooms. 7 wheelchair spaces across all levels.
